questions.label: Q1
questions.teaser: A. Describe sovereignty. B. Describe a way governments promote economic liberalization. C. Explain how economic liberalization policies can present challenges to sovereignty. D. Explain why a…
questions.promptText:
1. Respond to parts A, B, C, and D.
A. Describe sovereignty.
B. Describe a way governments promote economic liberalization.
C. Explain how economic liberalization policies can present challenges to sovereignty.
D. Explain why a government might adopt economic liberalization policies despite challenges to
its sovereignty.
questions.scoringGuide: AP Comparative Government FRQ 1 is Conceptual Analysis, 4 points, one per part (A–D), no stimulus. The task pattern: A describe a concept, B describe a way/example, C explain a relationship or challenge, D explain a why/motivation. Set 1 answer key: A [1] describe sovereignty (independent legal authority over a population/territory without outside interference). B [1] a way governments promote economic liberalization (privatize resources/state enterprises, reduce tariffs, join a free-trade agreement/IMF/WTO, create special economic zones, cut regulations). C [1] explain how economic liberalization can challenge sovereignty (foreign govts/MNCs exert pressure; complying with supranational trade rules; FDI cultural influence; environmental/inequality backlash). D [1] explain why a government adopts it despite the challenge (improves the economy → legitimacy; popular support; prestige/power; reduces poverty). Common failure: describing the opposite concept (e.g., nationalizing for economic liberalization), or a D-answer that states a benefit without linking it to why it is worth the sovereignty tradeoff.

rubric.name: Part A
rubric.criteria: Award 0–1 point for part A exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. A [1] describe sovereignty (independent legal authority over a population/territory without outside interference)

rubric.name: Part B
rubric.criteria: Award 0–1 point for part B exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. B [1] a way governments promote economic liberalization (privatize resources/state enterprises, reduce tariffs, join a free-trade agreement/IMF/WTO, create special economic zones, cut regulations)

rubric.name: Part C
rubric.criteria: Award 0–1 point for part C exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. C [1] explain how economic liberalization can challenge sovereignty (foreign govts/MNCs exert pressure; complying with supranational trade rules; FDI cultural influence; environmental/inequality backlash)

rubric.name: Part D
rubric.criteria: Award 0–1 point for part D exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. D [1] explain why a government adopts it despite the challenge (improves the economy → legitimacy; popular support; prestige/power; reduces poverty)

examples.label: Sample 1A
examples.summary: Q1 (Set 1) scored 4/4. A: sovereignty as the state's capability to create/enforce/regulate without outside interference. B: privatization of resources. C: economic liberalization gives outside forces (MNCs) control, reducing the state's influence over its economy. D: a government adopts it to join supranational organizations (World Bank/IMF) that provide aid and drive economic growth. Full-credit model across all four parts.

examples.label: Sample 1B
examples.summary: Q1 (Set 1) scored 3/4. Earned A (independence without outside interference), B (reduce tariffs), and C (accepting a larger state's help creates dependence/indebtedness). Lost D: said liberalization lets the government participate in free-market trade but never explained the benefit of that participation or why it is worth sacrificing sovereignty. Illustrates the common D-part gap — naming an action without its payoff/motivation.

examples.label: Sample 1C
examples.summary: Q1 (Set 1) scored 1/4. Earned only A (full power over the state with no external control). Lost B (described nationalizing industries, the opposite of economic liberalization), C (described allies sharing resources, not a challenge to sovereignty), and D (discussed industry revenue, not relevant to sovereignty). Illustrates that misdefining the core concept (liberalization vs. nationalization) cascades through the later parts.

questions.scoringGuide: AP Comparative Government FRQ 2 is Quantitative Analysis, 5 points, one per part (A–E), based on a data graph. Task pattern: A identify a value from the data, B describe a trend in the data, C describe a course concept, D draw a data-based conclusion, E explain what the data imply about a relationship. Set 1 answer key (Corruption Perceptions Index graph): A [1] country with highest perceived corruption in 2015 = Nigeria. B [1] describe China's CPI-score trend 2018–2021 (score increased / perceived corruption decreased). C [1] describe political legitimacy (people's belief that the government has the right to rule; sources include elections, transparency, tradition, performance). D [1] draw a conclusion explaining the UK's low perceived corruption (free/fair elections, transparency, consolidated democracy, rule of law). E [1] explain what the data imply about corruption vs. legitimacy in China (e.g., little correlation — high legitimacy from economic performance despite moderate corruption; or govt reduced corruption to maintain legitimacy). Common failure: for C, defining legitimacy as the ability to hold/maintain power rather than the people's belief in the right to rule; for D, restating score changes instead of giving a reason.

questions.label: Q3
questions.teaser: Compare the limits on the power of the judicial system in two different AP Comparative Government and Politics course countries. A. Describe a function of a judicial system. B. Describe a limit on…
questions.promptText:
3. Compare the limits on the power of the judicial system in two different AP Comparative
Government and Politics course countries.
Respond to parts A, B, and C.
A. Describe a function of a judicial system.
B. Describe a limit on the power of the judicial system in two different AP Comparative
Government and Politics course countries.
C. Explain why each of the two AP Comparative Government and Politics course countries
described in (B) would limit the power of their judicial systems.
questions.scoringGuide: AP Comparative Government FRQ 3 is Comparative Analysis, 5 points: A describe a concept (1), B describe/apply it in TWO different AP Comparative course countries (2, one per country), C explain WHY for each of those two countries (2, one per country). The six course countries are China, Iran, Mexico, Nigeria, Russia, and the UK. Set 1 answer key: A [1] a function of a judicial system (interpret laws, assess constitutionality, resolve disputes, apply law, checks and balances, protect rights, establish rule of law). B [2] describe a limit on judicial power in two course countries (e.g., China: judiciary under CCP control / rule by law; Russia: judges nominated by the President, no judicial review; UK: no judicial review, bound by common law; Iran: Chief Justice appointed by Supreme Leader). C [2] explain why each country limits judicial power (e.g., China/Russia: executive consolidates power / controls dissent; UK: parliamentary sovereignty / prevent any branch dominating; Mexico/Nigeria: checks and balances). Common failure: attributing powers a country's executive does not actually have; explanations that restate the limit rather than give a reason. Both B and C are country-specific — an inaccurate country claim loses that country's point in both.

rubric.name: Part A
rubric.criteria: Award 0–1 point for part A exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. A [1] a function of a judicial system (interpret laws, assess constitutionality, resolve disputes, apply law, checks and balances, protect rights, establish rule of law)

rubric.name: Part B
rubric.criteria: Award 0–2 points for part B exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. B [2] describe a limit on judicial power in two course countries (e.g., China: judiciary under CCP control / rule by law; Russia: judges nominated by the President, no judicial review; UK: no judicial review, bound by common law; Iran: Chief Justice appointed by Supreme Leader)

rubric.name: Part C
rubric.criteria: Award 0–2 points for part C exactly as the official 2025 scoring guideline for this question specifies. C [2] explain why each country limits judicial power (e.g., China/Russia: executive consolidates power / controls dissent; UK: parliamentary sovereignty / prevent any branch dominating; Mexico/Nigeria: checks and balances)

examples.label: Sample 3A
examples.summary: Q3 (Set 1) scored 5/5. A: judicial function = resolve civil and criminal disputes. B (both earned): UK lacks judicial review (cannot rule on constitutionality of Parliament's laws); Russia's judiciary lacks independence, judges nominated by the President. C (both earned): UK limits the judiciary to concentrate power in Parliament/executive and preserve policy continuity; Russia limits it so the executive (Putin) can consolidate power. Full-credit model with accurate, country-specific claims.

examples.label: Sample 3B
examples.summary: Q3 (Set 1) scored 3/5. A: judicial review of laws' constitutionality. B: 1/2 — UK point earned (advises Parliament via committees but cannot overturn laws); Russia point lost (incorrectly said Russia's judiciary 'doesn't have judicial review'). C: 1/2 — UK explanation lost (efficiency claim didn't clarify parliamentary sovereignty); Russia earned (limits judiciary so United Russia keeps one-party dominance and Putin consolidates power). Shows how one inaccurate country claim costs a point while the parallel country still scores.

examples.label: Sample 3C
examples.summary: Q3 (Set 1) scored 1/5. Earned only A (judiciary checks laws against the constitution). Lost both B points and both C points because it attributed powers the executives do not possess — claimed Nigeria's president can remove justices and Mexico's president can ignore judicial rulings. Illustrates that factually wrong country claims void both the description and explanation points for those countries.

questions.label: Q4
questions.teaser: Develop an argument about whether government protections of civil liberties increase or decrease stability in a state. Use one or more of the following course concepts in your response: •…
questions.promptText:
4. Develop an argument about whether government protections of civil liberties increase or
decrease stability in a state.
Use one or more of the following course concepts in your response:
• Democratization
• Transparency
• Rule of law
In your response you should do the following.
• Respond to the prompt with a defensible claim or thesis that establishes a line of
reasoning using one or more of the provided course concepts.
• Support your claim with at least TWO pieces of specific and relevant evidence from
one or more course countries. The evidence should be relevant to one or more of the
provided course concepts.
• Use reasoning to explain why your evidence supports your claim or thesis, using one or
more of the provided course concepts.
• Respond to an opposing or alternate perspective using refutation, concession, or rebuttal.
questions.scoringGuide: AP Comparative Government FRQ 4 is the Argument Essay, 5 points across four rows. Row A Claim/Thesis [1]: a defensible thesis establishing a line of reasoning that uses at least one required course concept. Row B Evidence [2]: two pieces of specific, relevant evidence from required course countries tied to a course concept (1 point each). Row C Reasoning [1]: explain how/why the evidence supports the thesis (requires the Row A point). Row D Alternate Perspectives [1]: describe an opposing perspective AND refute, concede, or rebut it (requires the Row A point; merely describing the alternate view is not enough). Set 1 prompt: whether government protections of civil liberties increase or decrease stability in a state, using one or more of democratization, transparency, and rule of law. Common failure: a 'thesis' that only restates the prompt (loses A); presenting an alternate view without refuting/conceding/rebutting it (loses D); evidence not tied to a course concept.

rubric.name: Claim / Thesis
rubric.criteria: A defensible thesis that establishes a line of reasoning and uses at least one of the required course concepts.

rubric.name: Evidence
rubric.criteria: One point per piece of specific, relevant evidence from the required course countries tied to a course concept (up to 2).

rubric.name: Reasoning
rubric.criteria: Explains how or why the evidence supports the claim or thesis.

rubric.name: Alternate Perspective
rubric.criteria: Describes an opposing or alternate perspective AND responds to it with refutation, concession, or rebuttal.

examples.label: Sample 4A
examples.summary: Q4 (Set 1) scored 5/5 (Thesis 1, Evidence 2, Reasoning 1, Alternate 1). Thesis: protections of civil liberties increase stability through transparency. Evidence: UK transparency during Brexit; Iran's media control/hijab enforcement → protests. Reasoning: government honesty builds trust that stabilizes the state. Alternate perspective: acknowledged the 'loss of control/factions' counterargument then rebutted it. Full-credit model for the argument essay.

examples.label: Sample 4B
examples.summary: Q4 (Set 1) scored 4/5 (Thesis 1, Evidence 2, Reasoning 1, Alternate 0). Thesis links protections to stability via transparency and rule of law. Evidence: Russia (rule by law, subjective punishments) and China (media censorship reducing transparency). Reasoning: reduced transparency undermines trust and stability. Lost Row D: presented an alternate argument but offered no rebuttal, refutation, or concession. Illustrates the most common argument-essay miss — describing the counterview without responding to it.

examples.label: Sample 4C
examples.summary: Q4 (Set 1) scored 2/5 (Thesis 0, Evidence 2, Reasoning 0, Alternate 0). Earned both evidence points (UK rule of law protecting civil liberties; Nigeria democratization with low transparency re: MOSOP). Lost the thesis point because the claim referenced 'fundamental principles of a democracy' without using democratization, transparency, or rule of law as the line of reasoning — and because Row A was not earned, Reasoning and Alternate Perspectives were ineligible. Illustrates how a thesis that omits the required course concepts caps the score even with strong evidence.
